intro:
These exercises move from modelling a peer protocol as owned events to defending real connectivity and transport-selection decisions. The thread running through all of them is the chapter's central correction: a peer-to-peer node is calmest when one owner holds the protocol state and everything that crosses an async or channel boundary does so as an owned value, not as a shared reference to live transport. Get that ownership boundary right and the swarm loop becomes a plain state machine you can drive without a socket; get it wrong and you inherit duplicate-state bugs, shutdown races, and unbounded resource growth.

The later exercises broaden the lens from one node to a deployed mesh. Discovery has to survive hostile and noisy inputs, connectivity has to work for peers that cannot accept inbound dials, and the choice to use P2P at all has to be defended against brokers and service APIs that may fit the workload better. The recurring senior judgement is to treat NAT fallback, relay budgets, and convergence rules as product and operational concerns rather than networking trivia, and to reach for a hybrid transport split when topology and durability pull in different directions.

exerciseSolutions.title: Model one tiny P2P protocol as events and state transitions
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Split the protocol into two streams of owned values: local commands that your application issues downward, and network events that the transport delivers upward. The network edge produces events — ConnectionEstablished, Response, Gossip — because they are facts that already happened on the wire. Local application logic produces commands — Dial, SendRequest, Publish — because they are intentions you want the swarm to act on. Keeping these as separate enums is the whole design: the state machine has exactly two doors, on_command and on_event, and both take &mut self so there is one owner and no shared mutable transport handed around.

The identifiers that must thread through the machine are the PeerId and the request_id. The PeerId is the stable correlation field for connection and gossip events; the request_id is the stable correlation field for the request/response pair. Without the request_id you cannot match a Response back to the SendRequest that created it, and you cannot tell a duplicate or late response from a fresh one.

For pending work, the rule is simple: SendRequest adds a pending entry keyed by request_id, and the matching Response clears it. Dial and ConnectionEstablished move a peer toward the connected set but add no pending request; Publish and Gossip add no pending state at all because pub-sub is fire-and-forget news rather than a question that expects one answer. The transitions that add pending work are the ones that expect a reply; the transitions that clear it are the replies.

To make the sequence replayable in a deterministic test, record the ordered list of events and commands as plain values plus the resulting state snapshot (connected count, pending count, last log line). Because every input is an owned value rather than a live socket, another engineer can feed the same Vec of events into a fresh SwarmState and get byte-identical output — that reproducibility is the payoff of modelling the protocol as owned events instead of shared transport access.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Local commands and network events as separate owned enums, with the correlation fields called out.
criteria: Local commands (Dial, SendRequest, Publish) are a distinct enum from inbound network events (ConnectionEstablished, Response, Gossip).
SendRequest is identified as the transition that adds a pending-request entry, and ConnectionEstablished as the one that adds a connected peer.
request_id and PeerId are named as the stable correlation fields carried through the machine.
The replay argument turns on every input being a plain owned value rather than shared access to a live transport.

exerciseSolutions.title: Identify ownership and async-task boundaries in a swarm loop
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The swarm loop itself should own the swarm directly. In the libp2p shape from this chapter, the swarm is the outer machine that owns connections and does the polling, and exactly one task should drive it inside a select! whose two arms drain the two owned input streams: application commands coming down, and network events coming up. That task is the single writer of outbound transport effects. The broad shared lock in the inherited node is a symptom — it exists only because the design failed to pick one owner, so it papers over the missing ownership boundary by serialising every accessor instead.

Application state should have its own owner, separate from the swarm. The chapter is explicit that the swarm is not your business object and a behaviour is not your whole node: network orchestration and domain state belong in different places so tests can drive protocol state machines without real sockets. Practically, the swarm-driving task holds &mut node.state and is the only thing that mutates protocol maps and queues; the application reaches that state only by sending owned commands across a channel, never by grabbing a reference to the live connection.

The data that should cross boundaries as owned values is everything the unrelated tasks currently mutate in place: a task that wants to send a request should enqueue a SendRequest command rather than write to a transport handle, and a task that reacts to a response should receive a Response event rather than read shared connection state. Once one writer owns outbound effects, the outbound path becomes trivial to reason about — message ordering on the wire is just the order the single owner dequeues commands, and there is no interleaving of half-written frames from competing tasks.

The cancellation and shutdown bug that becomes far more likely with many partial owners is a double-free-style race on connection lifecycle: several tasks each believe they own the connection, so on shutdown one closes it while another is mid-write, or two tasks both try to dial-then-tear-down the same peer and the protocol state ends up describing a peer that is simultaneously connecting and disconnected. With one owner, cancellation is a single decision made in one place, and duplicate or contradictory state transitions cannot occur because only one &mut self ever applies them.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One task owns both the swarm and the protocol state; other tasks reach it only through owned commands.
criteria: The swarm-driving task is named as the owner of the swarm, and SwarmState (domain state) is given a distinct owner so tests can run without sockets.
Outbound work is proposed as owned LocalCommand values sent over a channel rather than writes to shared transport handles.
The single-writer arrangement is tied to deterministic outbound ordering and to eliminating duplicate/contradictory state transitions.
The shutdown hazard is framed as a connection-lifecycle race among tasks that each think they own the connection, resolved by one owner with one shutdown point.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a small libp2p-style swarm loop over owned enums
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Model the node as one plain struct, SwarmState, that owns three pieces of state: the set of connected peers, a map of pending requests keyed by request id, and a log queue for observability. There is no Rc, no RefCell, and no raw pointer in the main design — single ownership through &mut self is exactly what makes the loop testable, and it mirrors the ownership story many real libp2p nodes want internally.

The pending-request map is the honest core of the design. A SendRequest (or, in the lab's reduced vocabulary, a Request event) inserts an entry keyed by request_id whose value is the peer the request went to. The matching Response removes that entry. Because insertion and removal are keyed by the same id, the size of the map is always the count of genuinely in-flight requests; you cannot accidentally report a request as still pending after its response, and you cannot clear a request that was never issued. That keyed insert/remove pair is the simplest mechanism that keeps response handling truthful.

Connection events append to the connected collection, and every transition pushes a human-readable line onto the log queue. Reading the log back gives a deterministic trace of what the node did, which is what lets the runnable lab assert connected = 1, pending = 0, and a final log line of response peer-b state-v3 without any live transport. The whole point is that the same owned enums that would cross async or channel boundaries in a real node also drive this in-memory machine unchanged.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One owner, one pending map keyed by request id, one log queue — the same shape a real libp2p node wants internally.
criteria: SwarmState is the single central owner of connected peers, pending requests, and the log.
Request inserts a pending entry keyed by id and Response removes it, so pending count tracks genuinely in-flight work.
The log queue records each transition, letting the lab assert connected, pending, and the final line deterministically.
The design uses plain ownership with no Rc/RefCell/raw pointers, so it is testable without a live network.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair peer discovery with abuse controls and observability
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that discovery is unbounded and unmeasured: it accepts every advertised peer, queues unlimited dials, and emits no telemetry, so it is both a correctness problem and a resource-exhaustion problem. Discovery treats hostile input as trusted input, which in a P2P system is exactly backwards — any peer can advertise any other peer.

Dedupe belongs in both places, against two distinct kinds of waste. A known-peer set prevents re-processing a peer you already know about and stops a flood of repeated advertisements from doing repeated work. A pending-dial set prevents queuing a second dial for a peer that already has one in flight, which is the dedupe that actually bounds the dial queue. They guard different failure modes — duplicate discovery versus duplicate dialing — so you want both.

Validation must run before any expensive work. Cheap rejection means checking the advertised record before you allocate a dial or touch the queue: reject malformed or non-routable multiaddrs, reject self-advertisements, reject peers already in the known set, and reject anything over the per-source advertisement budget. All of these are constant-time checks that cost nothing, and doing them first means a hostile peer cannot make you spend a dial slot or an allocation just by sending a record. The explicit budgets to make first-class are a maximum pending-dial queue depth, a per-peer dial-attempt cap with backoff, and a cap on accepted advertisements per source per interval.

For observability, instrument at minimum the dial-failure count (by reason), the relay-fallback usage rate, and the age of the oldest pending dial; duplicate-discovery rejections and current pending-dial depth are valuable additions. The oldest-pending-dial age is the early warning that the queue is backing up faster than it drains, and relay usage is the signal that the mesh is silently degrading. A good test or simulation case feeds a burst of thousands of advertisements for the same handful of peers plus a stream of unreachable addresses, and asserts that the pending-dial queue never exceeds its bound, that duplicate advertisements are rejected without new dials, and that dial-failure and relay-usage counters move as expected.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two dedupe sets, an explicit pending-dial budget, cheap validation first, and metrics on every drop path.
criteria: Adds dedupe in both the known-peer set and the pending-dial set, plus an explicit max-pending-dial budget.
Routability/known/self checks run before any dial or allocation work, rejecting bad records cheaply.
Names at least three observability hooks: dial-failure count, relay-fallback usage, and oldest-pending-dial age.
Gives a simulation case: an advertisement flood plus unreachable addresses asserting bounded queue depth and correct counters.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design NAT traversal, relay fallback, and connectivity telemetry
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Every peer attempts the connectivity ladder in the same order, but the realistic outcome depends on where the peer sits. The default is direct dial first: a node tries the peer's advertised address directly. Cloud VMs with public routable addresses will usually accept this; laptops and branch-office devices behind NAT usually will not accept unsolicited inbound. When the direct dial fails, the node attempts hole punching (coordinated simultaneous dial using observed addresses) to establish a direct path through both NATs. Only when hole punching also fails does it fall back to a relay, where a third public peer forwards traffic. The relay is the escape hatch of last resort, not the first choice — it is exactly the dangerous silent default the chapter warns about.

The retry and lease policy for repeated direct-dial failures should be capped exponential backoff with a per-peer attempt budget, and relay circuits should be held on a short lease that is periodically re-challenged with a fresh direct-dial or hole-punch attempt. The reason to keep re-attempting direct connectivity even after a relay succeeds is that a relayed circuit consumes scarce relay capacity; without a lease that forces periodic upgrade attempts, peers settle permanently onto relays and the limited relay capacity becomes the bottleneck for the whole mesh. Connectivity budgets — how many simultaneous dials, how many relay circuits, how long a circuit may live before re-challenge — have to be settled before you ever reason about application throughput, because a peer that cannot connect cannot move data at all.

The telemetry has to make accidental relay dependence visible, since that is the failure that does not announce itself. Required dashboard fields before rollout: relay-usage rate (fraction of active connections currently relayed, the single most important number), hole-punch success rate, direct-dial failure rate broken down by reason, oldest queued outbound connection age, and relay-circuit capacity utilisation. The proof that relay is becoming the default accidentally is a rising relay-usage rate combined with a falling hole-punch success rate; if both move together you are degrading toward an all-relay mesh and should alert before users report slowness. Grounding this in the deployment: laptops and branch devices are the ones that will lean on relays, cloud VMs are your likely relay providers, so capacity planning ties directly to the laptop-to-VM ratio rather than to any generic P2P ideal.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The connectivity ladder as one ordered policy, with relay leased and every rung counted.
criteria: Defines a direct-dial-first path and an explicit relay fallback path (with hole punching as the intermediate rung).
Specifies capped exponential backoff with a per-peer attempt budget plus a relay-circuit lease that forces periodic upgrade re-attempts.
Requires at least three telemetry hooks: relay-usage rate, hole-punch success rate, dial-failure rate, and oldest queued outbound connection.
Keeps the reasoning tied to the laptop/VM/branch deployment shape and capacity planning rather than generic P2P advocacy.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose P2P vs brokered messaging, gRPC, or HTTP for one product
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Match each boundary to what it actually needs from the transport — durability, topology, or operational cost — rather than to implementation taste, which is the chapter's standing point that P2P is not the advanced answer to every network problem.

The collaborative edge cache is the genuine P2P case. Its value is direct data exchange between geographically close peers, partial decentralisation so a node keeps serving when the central path is lost, and verifiable peer identity so caches can trust each other's content addressing. This is exactly the workload libp2p exists for: peer discovery and direct peer-to-peer data movement are real product requirements, not nice-to-haves. The data plane wants the overlay.

The internal durable task pipeline is the case against P2P. It wants durable replay and queue semantics — at-least-once delivery, ordered or partitioned consumption, the ability to replay after a consumer crash — which a message broker provides natively and a mesh does not. Building durability and replay on top of P2P would mean reinventing the broker badly. Use a broker (the Chapter 30 shape) and let it own delivery guarantees.

The public billing API is the case for a typed service contract or plain HTTP. It is a request/response boundary with external clients, strong auditability requirements, and a need for ordinary load balancers, gateways, and TLS termination. gRPC (Chapter 47) or HTTP gives you a typed contract and the entire operational ecosystem; overlay routing would add cost and obscurity with no benefit, since there is no peer discovery or decentralisation requirement here at all.

The edge cache is also where the hybrid split belongs, and hybrid is the calm senior answer when topology and durability pull apart. Run the control plane — membership, cache-policy distribution, health — over HTTP or gRPC to a central coordinator that is easy to operate and audit, while the data plane (the actual cached-object exchange) runs over libp2p between peers. The boundary splits cleanly along control versus data: centralised, durable, auditable control; decentralised, direct, high-volume data. That mirrors the chapter's recommended hybrid: HTTP/gRPC for control plane, a broker for durable work, and libp2p only where peer discovery and direct exchange are real requirements.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One transport decision per boundary, with the edge cache split into a hybrid control/data plane.
criteria: Picks the edge cache for P2P (direct exchange, partial decentralisation) and the task pipeline against it (durable replay/queue semantics belong in a broker).
Provides a hybrid design: HTTP/gRPC control plane plus libp2p data plane for the edge cache, split along control vs data.
Justifies each choice by durability, topology, or operational cost rather than implementation style.
States plainly that the billing API wants typed RPC/HTTP because overlay routing adds cost with no discovery or decentralisation benefit.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
connected = 1
pending = 0
last = response peer-b state-v3
labSolution.explanation:
The lab gives you a complete owned-event state machine with one branch left as a stub. SwarmState is the single owner of all protocol state — a Vec of connected peers, a HashMap of pending requests keyed by request id, and a VecDeque log — and on_event mutates it through &mut self, so there is exactly one writer and no shared transport access. Three owned Event values are fed in sequence, the same way real network events would arrive over a channel.

The repair is in the Response branch. A request inserts an entry into the pending map keyed by its id; the matching response must remove that same entry, otherwise the pending count would never return to zero and the node would report in-flight work that has actually completed. The fix is self.pending.remove(&id) followed by pushing a log line of the form "response peer-b state-v3". The pending map is the source of truth for outstanding requests, so removal on response is what keeps response handling honest.

Tracing the sequence: Connected(peer-b) pushes one peer onto connected, so connected.len() is 1. Request { id: 7 } inserts key 7 into pending and logs "request 7". Response { id: 7 } removes key 7, leaving pending empty so pending.len() is 0, and pushes "response peer-b state-v3" as the final log entry. Reading log.back() therefore yields that last line. The program prints connected = 1, pending = 0, and last = response peer-b state-v3, matching the expected output exactly. It compiles and runs on the standard library alone because the whole point of the example is to teach the ownership model without a live transport.

reviewAnswers.question: Why do owned events and commands make a swarm loop easier to test than shared transport state does?
reviewAnswers.answer: When every input is a plain owned value — a LocalCommand or a NetworkEvent — you can feed a fixed sequence into a fresh state machine and get byte-identical output every run, because nothing depends on socket timing, lock acquisition order, or which task happened to mutate state first. Shared transport state, by contrast, requires a live connection or an elaborate mock to exercise, and its behaviour depends on interleaving you cannot control. With one owner mutating through &mut self there is a single place where state changes happen, so the test is just "apply these events, assert this snapshot." That is why the chapter's examples compile and run as ordinary Rust with no live network.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between peer identity, channel security, and application-level authorization?
reviewAnswers.answer: Peer identity tells you which cryptographic key is sending bytes — it answers "who is this" but says nothing about whether they should be trusted. Channel security (the encrypted, authenticated transport) guarantees the bytes were not tampered with or read in transit, but an authenticated channel to a malicious peer is still a channel to a malicious peer. Application-level authorization is the separate decision of whether this identified peer is allowed to make this particular request, with size checks, rate limits, and protocol permissions enforced regardless of how good the cryptography is. The chapter's point is that in P2P the attacker is on the inside: a valid identity and an encrypted channel are necessary but never sufficient, so you keep authorization checks even for cryptographically known peers.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are NAT traversal and relay fallback product concerns instead of networking trivia?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because most real users sit behind NAT that refuses unsolicited inbound connections, so whether a peer can connect at all is determined by your traversal strategy, not by application code — a node that cannot connect cannot deliver any product value. Relay fallback is a usable escape hatch but a dangerous silent default: if peers quietly settle onto relays, scarce relay capacity becomes the mesh bottleneck and the network degrades without any error surfacing. That makes relay-usage rate, hole-punch success, and dial-failure rate operational metrics you must watch before rollout, and it makes the retry/lease policy a capacity-planning decision. Connectivity budgets therefore matter before application throughput budgets do.

reviewAnswers.question: When is a deterministic scalar version plus tie-break rule enough for sync, and when is it too weak?
reviewAnswers.answer: A scalar version with a deterministic tie-break (higher version wins; on equal versions, the larger author id wins) is enough when updates are effectively sequential or when last-writer-wins is an acceptable semantics — all peers sharing the same merge rule will converge to the same value, which is the whole sync contract. It becomes too weak once you have genuine concurrent edits whose intent should be preserved rather than discarded: last-writer-wins silently drops one side of a true conflict, and a single scalar cannot represent that two changes happened independently. At that point you need stronger machinery — CRDTs, operation logs, or Merkle-based diffing — that captures concurrency instead of collapsing it to one winner.

reviewAnswers.question: What signs tell you a product really wants P2P instead of a broker or service API?
reviewAnswers.answer: The strong signals are a genuine need for direct peer-to-peer data exchange, verifiable peer identity, and partial decentralisation so nodes keep functioning when the central path is lost — for example an edge cache where nearby peers should serve each other directly. If instead the workload wants durable replay, ordered or partitioned consumption, and at-least-once delivery, it wants a broker, and reinventing those guarantees over a mesh is a mistake. If it is a typed request/response boundary with external clients and audit requirements, it wants gRPC or HTTP and the standard operational ecosystem. The honest answer is frequently hybrid: HTTP/gRPC for the control plane, a broker for durable work, and libp2p only on the data plane where discovery and direct exchange are real requirements.
